summary: An Gèadh is a short mystery game made in Unreal Engine 5. The player is an agent sent to an empty island city on Mars to recover a sample from the Viking 1 lander, an abandoned NASA machine. By following clues, the player reaches Viking 1 on a cliff and meets an old woman whose reactions change through an emotion system we built. The game uses NASA’s real Viking lander 3D model and a Mars-length day to bring a historic mission back to life through story. It matters because it lets people explore the history of Mars exploration instead of only reading about it.
details:
What it is: a short mystery game about an abandoned NASA machine.

How it works: the player explores an empty island city, follows clues to Viking 1 on a cliff, and meets one old woman whose behavior changes through an emotion-evaluation system, inspired by research on emotion, hormones, and weather, that reacts to her actions and the player’s.

Tools: Unreal Engine 5 and C++, motion matching and mocap animation (C++ version of Epic’s GASP), python for automation map set waypoints animation assignment. Gameplay logic is event-driven (messages, overlaps and timers) with no Tick in our own logic. The old woman’s personality lives in Data Assets and one emotion bar that reacts to her actions and the player’s. A day-night and weather system uses baked data (temperature, humidity, wind, a Mars-length day).

Pre-existing: an NPC framework from our earlier projects (Kareem-Eltablawy/NPC-Realistic-Greeting-System). During the hackathon we heavily rewrote its logic around a new emotion-evaluation model with richer DataAsset connections, ready for more content.

Real and fictional: Viking 1 and its history are real NASA material; the story, the city and the final symbol are fiction.

Use of SI: We used Claude (an AI chatbot) in these ways:

  • Code: help writing and debugging Unreal Engine C++ code.
  • Automation: Claude wrote Python scripts that assign Data Assets, animations, and waypoints across the map, and that organize the project folders from the start. This replaced hundreds of manual drag-and-drop steps. The scripts saved time and did not design the game.
  • Research: we used it to gather and summarize background reports on how emotion, hormones, weather, and health are linked. These reports informed our emotion model, which is a simplified game system, not medical advice or clinical science.
  • Images: two images in our presentation slides were made with SI image tools, and each has a visible “AI-generated” watermark. The game itself contains no SI-generated images.
  • Impact: Players explore the real history of the Viking 1 mission through an interactive story.
  • Creativity: An emotion-driven character built from Data Assets, and gameplay logic with no Tick, using only events, overlaps, and timers.
  • No SI content uses NASA logos or branding. Our team created the game idea, story, and design.
